note: The weekly loop's first challengers, from the research (18 Nov 2026): what the research was unsure of, ranked, alternating first-second and look tests.

candidates.test: Shorts where every beat is understandable with the sound off: the line's verb is acted out by parts in the scene (part A visibly moves and pushes, carries, cuts or lights part B), input -> process -> output in one frame, the moving part on the spoken word; labels only name parts. Against the champion, where objects appear and the narration carries the cause.
candidates.why: Owner, 27 Nov, on L-20261127-21: 'I have to hear things properly to understand rather than seeing'. Its contact sheet bears it out: most frames are tiles, bars and cards appearing on a stage, with the operation itself (a token multiplied, a word picked) never shown happening. The week's biggest machine Shorts are the opposite: 'EVER WONDERED HOW A START MOTOR WORKS?' 280M views on 260K subscribers, 6 s; Science Scope's starter motor 50.0M on 121K, 15 s; 'Kick Start Mechanism' 6.84M on 61.9K, 9 s; Mevix lab's kick-start cutaway 767K on 385 subscribers in 4 days. All are near-wordless 3D cutaways where the gears push each other in order, so the picture alone tells the cause. An owner note asking for a change goes to the top of its kind.

candidates.test: Shorts whose camera holds one shot size per idea and drifts, pans or orbits inside it, changing size only on the word that reveals something (about one change every 4 s, never a push in and straight back out), against the champion's size change on nearly every word
candidates.why: The owner on the long video L-20261124-21: 'too many zoom in and zoom outs it was very difficult to actually keep an eye on whats happening'. That video changed size every 1.3 s; long videos now have a gate (renderer/craft.py camera_problems). Shorts change only through the loop, so this is the next look test. Research 2026-11-25 (pacing night): our last five Shorts give every 6 s beat 3 camera keys and 3 shot sizes (a size change about every 2 s) and a new place every beat (8-10 places a minute); the 13 reference Shorts under 100 s in research/sheets/ (Branch Education, Professor Of AI, Inside Decoded, AI Tech 3.7) hold a shot 4-6 s with one move or none (46% static, 33% push in), motion 1.5-1.9 of 3.

candidates.test: Shorts whose second and third lines go straight into the machine working (the 'how' answered with a moving part by 6 s: 'How? Its machines were 150 metres long and built the tunnel as they dug'), with no year, inventor backstory or historical figure before 10 s, against the champion, where the line after the question may open on a date or a record ('In 1945, radar engineer Percy Spencer...', 'Historically, it made up to 2,074 megawatts')
candidates.why: Our own retention: both Shorts with a curve lost their biggest share at 7.5 s, exactly on the line that turned to backstory: the microwave fell from 81% to 52% on 'In 1945, radar engineer Percy Spencer felt the chocolate...', Hoover Dam from 100% to 81% on 'Historically, it made up to 2,074 megawatts'. The Crossrail Short, whose second line was the machine itself, has 1,362 views in its first day, 5x our next best (284). References agree: 'How a Dam Generates Electricity' (AI Tech 3.7, 8.7M views on 11K subscribers, 41 s) is inside the intake at 0 s with no history; Inside Decoded's 'This computer had no chips' gives the twist at 2.4 s and the date only at 5-12 s. Two curves only, so medium confidence; placed first among first-second tests because it comes from our own drop points. Update research 2026-11-24: the transistor Short's curve is in and shows the same shape: its biggest drop, 24.5 points, is at 6.2 s on the second line 'The transistor. What did the very first one look like?', a re-asked question with no machine moving. Three curves of three now lose most at 6-8 s on a line that isn't the mechanism. Reviewer 2026-11-24: Crossrail's curve is in too: even it lost 15.4 points at 5.6 s on 'How? Its machines were 150 metres long', so four of four lose most at 5-8 s; a re-asked question there is now a lesson (lessons.md #1), the backstory half stays this test. Reviewer 2026-11-27: two more curves lost most on a backstory or date second line (Motorola brick −19 points at 5.5 s on 'Its engineers had just 6 weeks...'; Paris Metro −20.9 at 6.1 s on 'Paris first tried it in 1951. So what keeps it...'), on top of the microwave's −29.6. With three Shorts over 15 points, the backstory half is now lessons.md #1 too, so the writer already follows it; this test may be redundant (the improver decides whether to retire it).

candidates.test: Shorts titled as a plain statement that names the thing and promises the mechanism, with no question mark ('How Hoover Dam Makes Electricity', 'How the First Transistor Switched', 'Inside a Crossrail Tunnel Boring Machine'), against the champion's question title ('Why Does Hoover Dam Need Lake Mead to Be Full?'). The answer still waits: no figure and no payoff in either title.
candidates.why: In this channel's formats.json, 16 of the 19 reference videos at 500K+ views use a statement title ('How Electrical Outlets Work' 77.3M, 'How a Dam Generates Electricity' 8.7M, 'How Starlink Actually Works' 4.6M, 'How GPUs Are Printed With Light' 1.0M) and 3 a question (median 4.6M against 2.1M); the week's biggest on-profile breakout is titled 'NVIDIA's First Chip' (1.78M on 29.8K subscribers). All 8 of our Shorts so far use a question title, following the shared planner rule that came from money Shorts (13 of 20 asked). Medium confidence: reference titles, not a test inside our channel.

candidates.test: the payoff's figure as a picture in the first 3 s (a line diving to a number) against the champion's picture-first open
candidates.why: ColdFusion opens on the figure; only 11% of the niche's Shorts show a figure by 3 s

candidates.test: a 3D character skit Short against the champion zoom/invention Short
candidates.why: AI skits median 1.14M, but all 81 from one channel (Professor Of AI); needs the 3D character

candidates.test: 30-40 s Shorts against the 45-60 s champion
candidates.why: the scan's 20-35 s band hits 21% vs 11-12% at 35-70 s; the references run 58-97 s

candidates.test: a look morph (textured -> wireframe -> clay -> textured) as the opening picture
candidates.why: the owner's favourite reference opens on it

candidates.test: a contradiction slammed in big at 0.5 s ('NO CHIPS') instead of the question line
candidates.why: Inside Decoded's water-computer Short opens this way; 2 of 19 references

candidates.test: a light, clean studio stage instead of the dark one
candidates.why: Branch Education's Shorts mix light gradient stages; the dark stage is the champion from the long references

candidates.test: titles that name the thing in the third person, with no 'you' or 'your' ('Why Keyboards Aren't in ABC Order'), against titles that address the viewer ('Why Your Keyboard Isn't in ABC Order')
candidates.why: Niche scan of 3,594 tech Shorts (niche-data 2026-11-18): titles with you/your have a median 0.81x their channel's median views and 20% hits (n=426) against 1.02x and 31% without; lower inside 19 of 29 channels that use both (Inside Decoded 0.46x vs 1.71x over 31 titles). Three of our open topics use 'Your'. Views are the evidence; the loop judges it on stayed to watch.

candidates.test: invention Shorts titled as a numbered series ('The Inventions Inside Every Phone, Part 3: The Transistor') against the champion's single claim title
candidates.why: Numbered-series titles: 1.46x channel median, 44% hits (n=25) against 1.0x and 30%; higher inside 4 of 5 channels that use them. Logibu's 'Most Important Invention In History, Part N' reached 5.35M and 3.96M on 36K subscribers. Mostly one channel, so low confidence.

candidates.test: Shorts told as the small-to-giant shape (an everyday thing the viewer holds, stepped up through real machines to the giant one) against the champion's one-thing-all-the-way-down story
candidates.why: You Built A... (12K subscribers) runs every Short this way: 'How a Stack of Bricks Becomes a Skyscraper' 2.53M views (211x its subscribers), its next 11 at 62K-508K (5-42x) in the 18 Nov niche scan. One channel only and 100-130 s long, so low confidence; placed last among first-second tests.

candidates.test: Shorts with about 20 machine sound effects a minute (channel.json sound.sfxPerMinute.short 20 on the test side; a tick, thud, glass or whoosh on every part that moves, clicks, lights or snaps, from the channel's own synthesized set) against the champion's cap of 12
candidates.why: The two AI-voiced 3D Shorts with the biggest outliers in our shot sheets run far denser sound than we do: AI Tech 3.7's 'How a Dam Generates Electricity' (8.6M views on 11K subscribers) about 20 effects a minute, Inside Decoded's Shorts 30-32 a minute; Branch Education (2.8M subscribers) 8-12, Professor Of AI about 10. Our cap is 12 and our five Shorts mix effects at -29 to -31 dB mean, 12 dB under the voice. Our held-after-hook is low (end hold 11-30%). Sound counts were estimated by eye in the built-in browser, and the dam sheet's sound probe was cut short, so confidence is low; placed after the light and morph look tests.

candidates.test: Shorts that keep one machine in one cut-open place for the whole explanation, the camera moving along and into it (Crossrail: the tunnel boring machine from wheel to chamber to conveyor to ring), against the champion, where beats may jump to a new place each line (microwave: kitchen, lab, tube, inside the tube, a popcorn kernel, a workshop, a showroom).
candidates.why: Held after the hook: Crossrail, which stayed on one machine in one place, 46.5%; the transistor (bench, then chip, then oscilloscope, then graphics card) 26.4%; Hoover Dam (dam, intake, powerhouse, turbine pit, generator, control room) 13.1%; microwave (seven places) 10.7%. Four Shorts and different topics, so no lesson yet: a look test. Research 2026-11-25: Crossrail, the one-machine Short, held 0.73 of its post-hook audience to the end (endHold) against 0.11, 0.15 and 0.32 for the microwave, dam and transistor Shorts that change place every beat (metrics/analytics.json); four Shorts only, so a test, not a rule. Reviewer 2026-11-27: three more Shorts fit the order: Paris Metro (one train, mostly under its own car) held 35.4% after the hook; NVIDIA (stage, chip, drafting table, old PC, game shelf, data hall) 31.5%; Motorola brick (studio, workbench, city at night, sky, street, shop, timeline rail) 29.8%. Crossrail's 45.5% is still the best. Seven Shorts, still a test.

candidates.test: Keep zoom-inside Shorts at most 2 in 5 until one of ours proves the shape; their only Short references are Branch Education's (504K-1.0M views on 2.78M subscribers, 0.2-0.4x), which check-plan rejects as demand. Tonight's zoom topics now cite Silicon Up Close's 'What Happens Inside an AI Chip When You Ask a Question' (1.02M on 12.7K, 80.6x) and PROCESS BHARAT's chipmaking video (2.2M on 234K, 9.4x).
candidates.why: plans built on zoom topics pass check-plan; the mix leans on invention Shorts, whose references are real breakouts

candidates.test: Check why the owner's pace fix (voice speed 0.92 -> 1.0, 'about 164 words a minute', commit 8cae8f7) lands at 140-148 words a minute in the three Shorts made since (timeline.json words over duration: transistor 148, Crossrail 140, mobile phone 148; microwave at 0.92 was 130). The gap is likely the beat pads and pauses between beats (channel.json beatPad, TEMPOS short 1.2). If the owner's note meant the spoken pace, close it (shorter pads, not a faster voice); if a pace change beyond that is wanted, it is a weekly-loop test on TEMPOS.
candidates.why: The owner's addressed pace note actually delivered; 5 of 16 reference Shorts in our sheets are 'fast' narrators
